summary:
BodyMap: Crew Health is a web app that helps astronauts check their own health on long missions and decide what to do next. An interactive human figure shows eight body systems: heart, eyes and brain, bones and muscles, immune system, metabolism, mind and sleep, balance, and radiation. Each is color-coded green, amber or red, always with an icon and a word. Tapping a system shows its readings, trends over the mission, why it changes in space, how to measure it, and clear next steps.

A 2-minute daily check-in collects 28 indicators drawn from NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency research, such as blood pressure, temperature, sleep, mood, vision and radiation dose. Follow-up questions appear only when an answer calls for them. A notification bell and routine page prompt rechecks, weekly tests, and checks after spacewalks or landings.

Guidance adapts to the mission. On the ISS, a red status means "call the flight surgeons now." On the way to Mars, with up to 20 minutes of delay each way, the crew is guided to act first. As missions go farther from Earth, astronauts must spot and handle health problems themselves, and BodyMap is built for that.
details:
What it does

BodyMap: Crew Health is a web app astronauts can use to check their own health during long missions and decide what to do next.

  • Body map. The home screen shows a human figure with eight body systems: heart and circulation, eyes and brain (SANS), bones and muscles, immune system, metabolism and nutrition, mind and sleep, balance and orientation, and radiation exposure. Each pin is green, amber or red, always with an icon and a word (OK, Watch, Act) and the latest reading. A summary and an alert strip put anything that needs action first.
  • System detail. Tapping a system opens a panel that leads with what to do now, then shows each indicator's reading, trend charts over the mission, step-by-step "how to measure" guides, and why that system changes in space.
  • Daily check-in. A 2-minute check-in asks one question per screen, and most answers take one tap. Follow-up questions appear only when an answer calls for them: a headache opens vision questions, and a fever opens symptom questions. Weekly items such as near vision, strength, body mass and radiation dose are spread across the week.
  • Mission routine. A notification bell and a Routine page list what to do next, most urgent first: a recheck after an abnormal reading (e.g. temperature again in 4–6 hours), checks after a logged spacewalk or landing, the daily check-in, and weekly tests.
  • Mission-aware guidance. Crews can switch between ISS, Artemis lunar and Mars transit profiles. The communication delay, radiation budget and escalation advice change with the mission. On the ISS, a red status means "call the flight surgeons now." On the way to Mars, with up to 20 minutes of delay each way, the crew is told to start the onboard protocol first, with the crew medical officer leading care.

How it works

Health content is kept separate from the code: 28 indicators, their thresholds, recommended actions and mission profiles.

  • Statuses. A rules engine scores each reading against bands and the astronaut's own baseline, then applies multi-day trend rules (e.g. a fever on two days in a row). A system takes the status of its worst indicator.
  • Check-in questions. A check-in engine builds the questions from the answers given so far.
  • Tasks. A scheduler turns readings, logged events and statuses into the day's tasks.
  • Demo crew. Three demo crew members have generated mission histories, so the app shows real trends right away. Users can also add their own profile, and their data stays in the browser.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Earlier detection. Regular, low-effort self-checks catch drift (rising temperature, worsening near vision, missed exercise) before it becomes a crisis.
  • Clear next steps. Every status comes with an action, not just a number. That matters most when the ground can't answer quickly.
  • Less burden. Questions are skipped when they aren't needed, numbers are pre-filled from the last reading, and nothing is forced.
  • Prepared for autonomy. As missions go farther from Earth, astronauts must handle more of their own care. BodyMap is a model for how health software can shift guidance from "ask the ground" to "act first, then report."

Tools and technologies

  • Language: TypeScript.
  • Framework and build: React with Vite.
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS, with a custom mission-control theme.
  • Charts: Recharts.
  • Routing and state: React Router and Zustand.
  • Dates and icons: date-fns and lucide-react.
  • Testing: Vitest and Testing Library, with over 400 unit and component tests.
  • Code quality: oxlint and Prettier.
  • Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: none needed. It runs in any browser on a phone, tablet or laptop, with no login and no backend.
  • AI assistance: developed with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

How it is creative

  • The human figure is the interface. Pins sit on the body regions they describe, with organ hints that light up in their status color, so the health picture reads at a glance.
  • Guidance depends on distance from Earth. The same red reading gives different instructions on the ISS, near the Moon and on the way to Mars.
  • Health monitoring as a mission routine. The app is built around a daily check-in, rechecks and event-driven tasks, much like the routines astronauts already follow, rather than one-off data entry.

Factors we considered

  • Grounded in research. Each indicator is traced to NASA Human Research Program or Canadian Space Agency sources and marked as direct (18), proxy (9) or added (1). The 48 sources are cited in the app.
  • Measurable in flight. Every indicator is something an astronaut can check with onboard tools or a self-test, with instructions for each.
  • Accessibility. Status is never shown by color alone. The app works fully by keyboard and screen reader, meets WCAG AA contrast, and works on phones through to desktops.
  • Safety and honesty. Thresholds are illustrative demo values, and the app says clearly that it isn't medical advice.
  • Privacy. No accounts and no server. Personal entries stay on the device.
  • Onboarding. A short welcome and a 6-step guided tour, plus first-time hints, because the challenge asks that astronauts not be assumed to know everything about assessing their health.
